posts.title: I Watched 'Capturing Bigfoot' — This Is What It's Really About
posts.description: A frame from the "Patterson-Gimlin" film of an alleged California Bigfoot filmed in 1967. (Commons Wikimedia.com)( A lthough I put "Bigfoot" web bookmarks inside the "Wildlife" bookmark folder in my web browser, this is not a really a Bigfoot (or other cryptids ) blog. There was that possibly maybe-Bigfoot-adjacent experience in June 2022. I have one friend, a professional forestry technician, who swears those were real "tree structures." Me, I don't know. I'm still on the bubble, as I always was about the famous 1967 Patterson-Gimlin film: a minute-plus of silent 16mm color footage of an apparent upright hair hominid walking along a northern California creek. That short film was always an outlier. I know of some Bigfoot-seekers who say that the creatures cannot be caught on film or video (and only poorly in still photographs) because of their paranormal quality of being here one moment and gone the next. posts.title: Gray Foxes Doing What They Do
posts.description: Gray Fox with prey — a wood rat? I was checking out one of the trail cameras when I discovered that it had files in its internal memory, in addition to the SD card where photos and videos normally would be stored. They dated from 2019. I am not even sure of the location, but it would have been close to home. One, taken in low light on July 4, 2019, showed this fox with some prey animal in its mouth. A wood rat? A a baby squirrel? The infrared illumination makes for a soft image. This month, I put some overripe bananas, some pumpkins, and a little peanut butter on a boulder up on the mountainside. No bears showed up, but the foxes did, as did the deer. Some video clips: Fox checks out some bananas. Fox investigates pumpkin. Having snacked, the fox moves on. Getting daytime photos was a surprise. posts.title: Don't Rush To Clean Up Your Garden Beds!
posts.description: Toss it away -- or let it sit? I spent part of this afternoon pulling up dead tomato plants, dumping out the Walls O Water (at this altitude, we use them all season long), and putting away the wire cages. But should I have done that? There is a good eco-friendly case to made for saving all that work until spring — although the plastic "walls" need to be stored out of the weather. From the Give a Shit about Nature website — also an account on X.com: The Fall Cleanup Instinct and Why It’s Worth Questioning There’s nothing wrong with wanting a tidy garden. The issue is that fall cleanup, when done thoroughly, often wipes out habitat at the exact moment it’s being occupied. The stems that look dead and expendable in October are full of eggs and larvae that have nowhere else to go. Nebraska Extension notes that when hollow stems are cut and moisture seeps into the open ends, it can kill the eggs, larvae, and pupae of native bees living inside.
